title: Module 4: Ride in Flow — Stack Check

blocks.content:
"If you just ride for watts, you cap your enjoyment. If you get good at riding your bike, your enjoyment is endless."

Twelve core tools. This is the final exam — one scenario per tool. No trivia. Just riding.

blocks.question: The road turns rough and the front wheel begins to bounce. What helps you regain control?

options.text: Slow if needed, let arms and legs move, keep feet supporting you and hands securely on the bars
Set an exact 70% pedal weight and 3/10 grip
Lock both elbows
Accelerate across the rocks

blocks.explanation: Use a stable, flexible stance and a pace that leaves time to react. The cue does not require numerical weight or grip targets.

blocks.question: On washboard, you cannot read the terrain clearly. What is the first adjustment?

options.text: Reduce speed until you can see and steer, then relax your joints and reassess the line
Keep speed and perform a hip movement without looking ahead
Stare at the front axle
Close your eyes for a moment to reset

blocks.explanation: Visibility and control come first. The hip hinge may help the bike move beneath you, but it is not a substitute for slowing when you cannot see clearly.

blocks.question: The bike feels skittish on loose gravel. How should you use pressure notes?

options.text: Stop safely, check equipment limits and other possible causes, then compare a small setup change on a familiar route
Immediately drop 5 PSI while riding
Assume the tire sound proves pressure is too high
Ignore the handling because gravel always feels loose

blocks.explanation: Harshness has several causes. Pressure is one setup variable to test carefully; no single noise or fixed PSI change determines the answer.

blocks.question: On a descent, an obstacle appears close ahead. What should guide your response?

options.text: Look toward available space, keep inputs smooth, and slow when you have room
Hold a fixed focal point five seconds ahead and ignore nearby rocks
Jerk the bars toward the shoulder
Close the gap to the rider ahead

blocks.explanation: Scan early for hazards, but respond to what you can actually see. A close obstacle may leave little time for a large line change.

blocks.question: Mile 68. A wet gravel road leads into a sharp switchback. What is the most useful braking plan?

options.text: Look ahead and slow smoothly with both brakes before the turn while the bike is mostly upright
Keep speed and use hard braking only after leaning into the corner
Use only the front brake on the descent
Lock the rear wheel to turn the bike

blocks.explanation: Give yourself time and room before the switchback. Use both brakes gradually on the approach. As the bike leans, ease heavy pressure and keep room to make a gentle correction if the surface changes.

blocks.question: Mile 82. A sweeping gravel corner looks looser than you expected. What should you do on the approach?

options.text: Choose a clear line and slow to a pace you can manage before turning
Ride at a speed calculated from the surface label
Carry the same pace and brake hard if the tire pushes
Use the outside lane even if you cannot see traffic

blocks.explanation: Use the Corner Check: read the visible surface and exit, choose an open line, and slow while mostly upright. There is no fixed safe percentage for a changing gravel bend.

blocks.question: The rear tire slips on a loose climb. What is a useful adjustment?

options.text: Shift to an easier gear, pedal smoothly, and use a position that keeps both tires tracking
Always stay seated on every gradient
Stand and sprint through the slip
Drop tire pressure while still riding

blocks.explanation: Smoother pedal force and a suitable gear may help. Test body position carefully; no universal grade determines whether sitting or standing is best.

blocks.question: You see a transition to looser gravel ahead. What is the useful sequence?

options.text: Read the visible surface, choose a clear line, slow if needed, and keep a flexible stance
Maintain speed because you saw the change early
Use a fixed 50-meter rule regardless of sightline
Look only at the riders behind you

blocks.explanation: Adapt to the surface you can see. The time and distance available vary with speed, visibility, and the riders around you.

blocks.question: Mile 118. You are on a smooth descent with a rider ahead and a bend farther down. What matters most before changing your position?

options.text: Keep a clear sightline, room behind the rider, and secure access to both brakes
Close the gap to a fixed drafting distance
Use a full tuck to claim a measured drag reduction
Take your hands away from the levers on the straight

blocks.explanation: The Position Ladder begins with control. Use a hand and body position you have practiced, keep enough room to see, and be ready to slow before the bend.

blocks.question: Mile 125. A group turns from firm gravel onto a loose section. You cannot see around the rider ahead. What do you do?

options.text: Open the gap until you can see and choose a line, even if the group moves away
Close the gap to protect the draft
Overlap the rider ahead to look around them
Hold a fixed following distance from the previous surface

blocks.explanation: The Elastic Gap gives you room to read a rough surface and react without abrupt inputs. You can regroup when the line becomes clear again.

blocks.question: You stop for a puncture. What comes before choosing a repair?

options.text: Move clear of traffic, identify the damage, and follow your tire and repair-kit instructions
Assume every visible hole is plug-safe
Use all your CO2 before inspecting the tire
Ride immediately if sealant sprays

blocks.explanation: Inspect the location and size of the damage before choosing a plug, tube, tire boot, or other fallback. Verify the repair and inflation before riding.

blocks.question: Late in a ride, your line choice and braking become less consistent. What should you do?

options.text: Slow down, create space, check your focus and body position, and stop or walk if control does not return
Keep riding at the same speed until the next timed reset
Ignore it because technique always recovers on its own
Follow the rider ahead more closely

blocks.explanation: Fatigue can change how you ride. Reduce the task demands and make a fresh assessment; stop or walk when you cannot steer and brake reliably.

blocks.content:
You built 12 core tools throughout the course:

1. The Weighted Drop
2. The Hip Hinge
3. The Pressure Window
4. The Quiet Eye
5. The Braking Sequence
6. The Corner Check
7. The Torque Ceiling
8. The 50-Meter Scan
9. The Position Ladder
10. The Elastic Gap
11. The Calm Hands Sequence
12. The 20-Minute Reset

This course is training wheels you're meant to grow out of. The drills stop being drills and become how you ride. The checklists stop being checklists and become automatic. The tools stay — they're yours now.

Go ride.
